content: In 1843, Emil Du Bois-Reymond, a German physiologist, was the first to describe action potentials associated with muscular contraction. He utilized a highly sensitive galvanometer containing over 5 kilometers of wire. Du Bois-Reymond also introduced the naming of different waves, using o to represent stable equilibrium and employing the letters P, Q, R, and S to describe various waveforms. In a later paper titled Naming of the Waves in the ECG, Dr. Willis Hurst credited Willem Einthoven for being the first to use the letters P, Q, R, S, and the additional T wave in electrocardiography. In 1850, M. Hoffa demonstrated that irregular ventricular contractions could be induced in canine hearts by administering electrical shocks. In 1872, Alexander Muirhead attached wires to the wrist of a febrile patient to record the patient’s heartbeat while pursuing his Doctor of Science degree in electricity at St. Bartholomew’s Hospital. This activity was directly recorded and visualized using a Lippmann capillary electrometer by British physiologist John Burdon Sanderson. In 1887, Augustus Waller, an English physiologist working at St. Mary’s Hospital in Paddington, London, published the first human electrocardiogram. He used a capillary electrometer connected to a projector, which allowed the heartbeat trace to be projected onto a photographic plate, enabling real-time recording of cardiac activity. In 1893, Willem Einthoven introduced the term electrocardiogram. By 1895, he described how he used a galvanometer to visualize the heart's electrical activity. The major breakthrough came in 1901 when Einthoven, working in Leiden, Netherlands, developed the string galvanometer, which was significantly more sensitive than the capillary electrometer used by Waller. Einthoven connected electrodes to a patient and demonstrated the electrical differences between two electrodes on the galvanometer. This innovation laid the foundation for modern electrocardiography, and the term Einthoven’s leads is still used today. The string galvanometer became the first clinical instrument for recording ECGs. In 1906, Einthoven assigned the letters P, Q, R, S, and T to the various deflections observed in the ECG and described the electrocardiographic features of several cardiovascular disorders. In the same year, he published the first article detailing a series of abnormal ECG patterns, including left and right bundle branch block, left and right atrial dilation, the U wave, notching of the QRS complex, ventricular extrasystoles, ventricular bigeminy, atrial flutter, and complete atrioventricular (AV) block. In 1924, Willem Einthoven was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his groundbreaking discoveries in electrocardiography. His first publication on the ECG appeared in Pflüger’s Archiv in March 1895, and his string galvanometer is now preserved in the Science Museum in London. During his time, patients were required to immerse their hands in salt baths connected to electrodes to record their heart's electrical activity. In the modern era, while the fundamental principles of early electrocardiography remain in use, significant advancements have been made in instrumentation. Early cumbersome laboratory equipment has evolved into compact electronic systems, often incorporating computerized ECG interpretation. For example, the Cambridge Simplicscribe, popular in the 1950s and 1960s, utilized vacuum tube technology, while the Cambridge VS4 of the 1970s and 1980s employed solid-state technology. Today’s ECG equipment is even more advanced, offering greater precision and efficiency. Presently, traditional 12-lead ECGs provide limited anterior views of the heart. However, the development of 80-lead ECG technology allows for a 360-degree spatial analysis of the heart by placing leads on both the front and back of the patient. This innovation has the potential to enable faster and more accurate detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), thereby expediting the delivery of critical care. For example, an 80-lead ECG system provides a color-coded representation of cardiac electrical activity, offering a comprehensive view of the heart’s function.
